name: Blackish Red-Purple
lede: Blackish Red-Purple is a dark, muted plum, [[red-purple|Red-Purple]] darkened almost to black by the modifier "blackish," the kind of compound name Robert Ridgway's 1912 nomenclature system built in long, regular families.

sections.title: A modifier on a named hue
sections.body:
The name follows the grammar "blackish" plus the parent hue [[red-purple|Red-Purple]]: the modifier marks a darkened, desaturated version of that base color, not a separate pigment or dye [1]. Robert Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912) first records a close match, at plate XII, hue 67, tone m [1]. The ISCC-NBS system picked it up again in 1955, filing it in block 259 under this same reddish-purple family [1].

Measured, the swatch reads as a dark grayish red by ISCC-NBS terms, about 5.5 units from the historical plate color, with Munsell notation 7.0RP 2.7/3.6 [1]. The closest look-alikes in our data are [[gooseberry|Gooseberry]], 3.4 units away, [[eggplant|Eggplant]], a purpler neighbor, and [[old-mauve|Old Mauve]], more vivid [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, finds this dark plum in 60 of them, about 0.25 percent, rarer than 58 percent of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1500s, at 1.5 times the expected rate for that century (5 of 2,231 paintings from then), and inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, 43 percent of the time, by lightness rank rather than raw area [2].

The earliest match in our archive is dated 1405, by the painter Starnina (Gherardo di Jacopo), 507 years before Ridgway's 1912 record [2]. Our archive's early centuries are thin, so that date is a floor, not a first, and the match is only a look-alike hue, not proof a matching dye or pigment existed then [2].
